newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian air export handling improves, imports suffe.
newsitem.headline: Indian air export handling improves, imports suffe.

text.p: NEW DELHI, March 14, Reuter - Cargo export handling at India's four main international airports has seen a marked improvement, with waiting times reduced significantly, Airports Authority of India (AAI)sources told Reuters.

But they also said the dwell time for import cargo at the four airports (Delhi, Bombay, Madras and Calcutta) has worsened to an an average stay time of 30 days from 21 days in the 12 months from January 1996.

For export cargo, however, the average stay time in last year was an average of five days and by this January it had been reduced to an average 2.2 days for 98 percent of cargo, and the remainder was now moved on the third day, they added.
Total import-export tonnage handled at all four international airports was 500,OOO tonnes in the 12 months to January 1997.
The sources said it was planned to cut the dwell time on imports.

This would be done in part by increasing charges and also by reducing the free period to two days from seven days in the course of 1998-- no date has been set, but the matter has already gone to the Standing Committee on Promotion of Exports by Air (the relevant government body), they added.

"The problem has been that consignees receiving import items have been treating the airports' cargo facilities as free or low-cost warehouses, either because they are cheaper than in town or they have no warehouses themselves anyway," the sources said.

"There is also a need to improve procedures. If the dwell times can be brought down to five days, for example, then we will have improved capacity effectively six times. In theory there would be no need for additional airport cargo space," they said.
It would also be improved if more bonded areas were developed, away from the airports, by Customs, and this was beginning to happen, they added.
"An airport cargo area should be for airport transit not storage", they said, and such bonded areas would help reduce pressure.

There was certainly a complex of factors influencing the speed of handling. Some suggested that it was a customs delay problem, but it was not that so much, the sources said, as, for example, the airlines not being able to communicate to with the consignee.

At the moment there was the seven-day free period for imports, then internal processing could add three to five days. But then one often found the consignee not willing to pay charges to receive. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
